frase_gancho.texto: A stone face with a trunk-like nose, begging for water in a land without rivers.

puente_narrativo.texto: Chichén Itzá, also in northern Yucatán, brings us back to a question we left in the Toltec Hall. Look for a reclining man who turns his head and holds a vessel on his belly.

guion_corto.texto: This limestone mask is more than a meter high and nearly a meter and eighty centimeters wide. It was part of the facade of the Codz Pop, a building at Kabah, in Yucatán, covered with hundreds of identical faces. It is Chaac, the Maya god of rain and lightning. Look at the nose: long, curved, coiled upward like a trunk. It has square eyes with a round center and curved fangs at the corners of the mouth. It is made of many pieces of stone, fitted together like a puzzle. In the Puuc region there are no rivers, so rain was everything. Each face was a plea to the sky.

guion_largo.texto:
What would you do if your whole world depended on the rain arriving on time? That is the question behind this face. The Puuc region, in the north of the Yucatán Peninsula, is an area of low hills, with no rivers or lakes. People lived off the rain, which they stored in underground reservoirs called chultunes. If the rain failed, everything was lost.

That is why Chaac, the god of rain and lightning, was the most important, and why his face was repeated everywhere. This mask is just one of the hundreds that covered the Codz Pop, a building at Kabah whose name means “rolled mat.” Imagine the entire facade, from top to bottom, with all those faces looking out: it was not decoration, it was a gigantic plea.

He is a Maya relative of the rain gods you have already met: [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo), of the Zapotec, and Tláloc, of the Mexica. The Maya called him Chaac. I told you in Oaxaca that here you would see a relative of his with the nose coiled upward, and there it is. All three cultures portrayed him with fangs and linked him to lightning and water. They are related gods, born of the same need.

The nose is the most striking feature. It has been said that it imitates the trunk of the tapir, an animal of humid regions. But not everyone agrees. Some specialists think it could also be the elongated nose of the sacred mountain, which the Maya called Witz. The small circles that appear on the forehead of some masks would indicate rock. The idea would be that clouds, maize seeds and sources of water came out from inside the hills.

Now think about how it was made. Each piece was cut to fit in only one place, and it is thought that each had a stone tenon at the back that sank into a core of lime and rubble, so that the mosaic was held fast to the wall. To assemble a complete facade, thousands of pieces were needed, and on top of that came the work of transporting and placing each one.

Kabah has another oddity: from a great arch of the city a white stone road began, a sacbé, which reached all the way to Uxmal, about twenty kilometers away. Anyone who traveled along it between the two cities, the one you have just seen and this one, passed from one to the other without leaving the same world of stone facades, Chaac and serpents.

And this way of asking for water is not only in the past. In many towns of Yucatán a ceremony to ask Chaac for rain is still held today, with offerings, prayers and shared food. Rain is still important, and so is the god.

Among the first travelers to describe this building were John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood, who visited it in the nineteenth century. Catherwood drew it. His drawings and their books showed many people, for the first time, that a complex civilization had existed in the Americas.

texto: Follow the great nose that coils upward
Look for the square eyes with a round center
Find the curved fangs at the corners of the mouth

texto.Dimensions: 1.11 m high x 1.79 m wide x 0.91 m deep

texto.pregunta: Myth: The trunk on the masks proves that the Maya knew elephants.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is the stylized nose of the god Chaac, related to the tapir or to the sacred mountain. The Maya never saw an elephant.
